title: The Runaway Rainbow Scarf
markdown:
Lulu the llama was having a lovely, quiet morning. Sunshine tickled her fluffy white wool. The air smelled sweet, like a daisy. She was eating yummy green clover that tasted like sunshine. Beside her, pecking at tiny seeds, was Peep the chick, a fluffy yellow ball with the happiest chirps. They were best friends: a big fluffy llama and a tiny brave chick.

Suddenly — whoosh! A flash of fuzzy rainbow colours zipped from the sky. It was a scarf, long and soft, with stripes of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple. It landed — plop! — right on Peep.

“Cheep! Help me out!” chirped Peep, wiggling like a tiny jelly bean under the warm wool. He could not see anything but fuzzy rainbow.

Lulu giggled. “Oh, Peep! You look like a little rainbow marshmallow. A surprised marshmallow.” Then her fluffy ears perked up. “Wait. That scarf looks like Professor Pipkin’s scarf.”

Professor Pipkin was their music teacher, a wise old owl with glasses that always slid down his beak. His lessons were like a fizzy drink of fun. And oh dear, it was almost time for music. It started in just one hour. Professor Pipkin did not like being late. Not one bit.

“We have to get this scarf back to him, Peep,” Lulu said, carefully lifting the woolly tangle off her friend. It felt warm and smelled a little like lavender and honey. “Come on. We need to be super quick.”

So off they trotted. Lulu took big happy steps. Peep took quick little hops, like a speedy drumbeat. The rainbow scarf was still in Lulu’s mouth, tasting of sunshine and lavender.

Whoosh went the wind, and away went the scarf.

Around the big friendly oak with the swing, a playful puff giggled through the leaves and snatched the scarf from Lulu’s mouth. It zoomed. It landed — bam! — right on Tegid the bunny’s twitching nose. Tegid had long floppy ears and was busy nibbling a crunchy carrot.

“Oh! Hello there!” squeaked Tegid, his nose wiggling like a tiny pink worm. “What is this soft thing on my face? It tickles my whiskers.”

“That’s Professor Pipkin’s scarf!” chirped Peep. “It flew away from us.”

Lulu gently nudged it off Tegid’s nose. “Sorry, Tegid. It’s a bit bouncy. We’re trying to get it back before music time.”

Tegid blinked. “Music time? Ooh, I love music. It makes my ears want to dance. Is it time yet?”

“Almost,” said Lulu. “Thanks, Tegid. You have lovely long ears.”

They hurried on. The scarf was like a silly kite.

Whoosh went the wind, and away went the scarf.

It zipped over the sparkly pond, where Fiona the frog was sunbathing on a big lily pad. Splish! It landed right on Fiona’s head, like a colourful fluffy hat. Fiona was dozing.

“Ribbit? What is this on my head?” Fiona asked, blinking her big googly eyes. “It’s so soft. Like a cloud fell down.”

“Professor Pipkin’s scarf!” peeped Peep, hopping onto the lily pad.

Lulu carefully took the scarf from Fiona’s green head. “Thank you, Fiona. We’re in a hurry.”

Fiona blinked. “Hurry? To music? Oh, I love music. It makes my toes tap, even though I don’t have toes.” She began a happy ribbiting song.

“Thank you!” called Lulu. With Peep trotting beside her, they kept going.

Whoosh went the wind, and away went the scarf.

It zoomed past a bushy hedge and landed — thump! — right on Bartholomew the badger, who was having a sleepy nap under a shady bush. Bartholomew had a snuffly nose, and he was not happy about waking up.

“Who goes there?” he grumbled, blinking. “Who put this fuzzy thing on my ear? It’s not a worm.”

Lulu felt a little wobble in her knees. “It’s us, Bartholomew. Lulu and Peep. And this is Professor Pipkin’s scarf, and it keeps flying away.”

Peep hopped right onto Bartholomew’s nose, which made the badger sneeze a soft sneeze. “We have to get it back. Music starts soon.”

Bartholomew yawned a giant yawn. “Music, you say? Well, that is important. My nephew loves music lessons. All right. Here you go.” He nudged the scarf gently. “Don’t let it escape again. It looks like a cheerful scarf.”

Lulu took it, feeling relieved. But the sun was high. The lesson was getting very close, maybe only ten minutes away. The path went up a grassy hill, and Lulu’s legs felt like wobbly jelly. “Oh, Peep,” she sighed, “I don’t think we can make it.” She really wanted to sit down and eat more clover.

Peep puffed out his tiny chest. “We can do it, Lulu. We’ve come so far. Remember Tegid’s wiggling nose, and Fiona’s happy ribbit song, and Bartholomew’s sleepy grumble. Professor Pipkin needs his scarf. Jelly can still walk.”

Peep’s cheerful chirps and silly jelly idea gave Lulu a burst of energy. They raced down the hill. Lulu’s legs pumped. Peep’s little legs were a blur of yellow fluff. They could see the little music school now, with its bright red door. Professor Pipkin stood just outside, looking a little concerned, glasses on the tip of his beak.

“Professor Pipkin! Professor Pipkin!” Lulu called, breathless. She held out the rainbow scarf.

His wise eyes widened. “My scarf! Oh, my dears. You found it. And you’re not late. You’re just in time.” He took it with a happy hoot. “Come in, come in. The lesson can begin.”

And so it did. Lulu and Peep sat on the soft rug and learned a new song about fluffy clouds. Lulu tapped her hooves with a happy thud-thud-thud. Peep tapped his tiny feet with a quick pitter-patter-pitter-patter. The rainbow scarf, for once, stayed put, warm around the owl’s shoulders, and the music went on.
